251.t: Paulie Christian and a Dallas band
251.s: Interviewer asks about Frenchie Christian; Albert's answer is garbled by ASR.
251.q: There was a little band in Dallas where Blaine Johnson was here. That's the one that Richard McCawfield and myself and Richard Johnson came. He was a very, very, very person that got sick and he would stop playing.

663.t: Guitarists around Tylertown and Jackson: Tommy Johnson, Bracey, McCoys
663.s: Questions about other guitar players in Mississippi, including Tommy Johnson, Ishman Bracey, the McCoy brothers, Big Joe Williams; he played with no one but Tom.
663.q: Did you hear Tommy Johnson play? I feel good. I know.

624.t: Asking about more musicians: Barth, Shannon, Newrock, Christians, Mendelson, Majada
624.s: Allen reads through names of local musicians and Brunies says what he knows of each: their playing, age, whether read by music, and neighbourhood ties.
624.q: He used to go on the love of Paul Young Abner. And he used to play with fish sometimes, you know. Sometimes when I couldn't make it, why, he went and played with fish. You remember Harry Shannon. Harry Shannon, yeah. He was an umpore player. He was an umpore player.

627.t: Good musicians he knew: Cal Williams and the Felters
627.s: Cage names Cal Williams, Frank, Joe and Artie Felters, near Staffly Station.
627.ch: Cage on work songs, church and social life
627.q: I know a whole lot of the Felters used to play a guitar. Joe Felters, Artie Felters. A whole lot of them used to play a guitar.

14.t: The Pickwick band and the Douroux family
14.s: Love recalls musicians in the old Pickwick band, including Dominguez and old man DeRooks, and the nephews of Dolly who play modern jazz.
14.ch: Funeral customs, Pickwick band and later years
14.q: Oh, that was a long time before my time. My father was a young man then. He used to come down here. I'll tell you some fellas was playing in that band. The country.

269.t: Jacques Villery collecting songs at the old folks' home
269.s: She recounts giving songs to young Jacques Villery at the home and discusses his family in the French Quarter.
269.q: It's not so long that I gave a young man, Villery. He had a box somewhat like that. And I was at the home. A la Sive des Vieillards, you know, old folks home.

690.t: Trenier's father, Willie Bolero and Thomas Daley
690.s: Pope names the father of the Trenier brothers and alto player Willie Bolero, called Chicken; the interviewer mentions Thomas Daley.
690.q: Bolero, like a Spanish name. Bolero, yes. And, of course, he was one of the late members, you know. He just trained him myself. He'd come along and go every day, you know. But my father practically gives it up.

128.t: Davy Jones, Joe Robichaux and Sam White
128.s: Short answers on who he played with: Joe Robichaux on road trips with Sam Morgan, and a few jobs with Sam White.
128.q: Who the old man? Young Joe. Young Joe. Oh. No, I never played with, yeah, I played with Joe, yeah, Joe played with me a couple of times with Sam Bang. We went on the road, Birmingham, different places, Mobile. Yeah, Joe played a couple of jobs with us.

905.t: Towns played in the country parishes
905.s: He played St. James, St. John and St. Charles parishes and Allen mentions musicians from that area.
905.ch: Country years in St. John Parish
905.q: Play music all different places. We are at Dansonville. When I was out there.

70.t: Wilbur De Paris, Vic Dickinson, Floyd Brady and J. C. Higginbotham
70.s: Jackson recalls Wilbur De Paris, Vic Dickinson of Xenia, Stump Brady who taught him and whose place he took with Zack White, and Higginbotham.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And, of course, Wilbur DeParis to me was a good trombone player, a very good trombone player. He was a what you call all-around trombone player. Vic Dickinson. Vic Dickinson left home before I did.
